enhanced_title: Studiers of Character and Food for Love
description: Mrs. Bennet visits Netherfield, much to Elizabeth's chagrin. A lively debate on poetry, the country, and 'intricate characters' ensues, while Lydia's demand for a ball sets the stage for future festivities.

analysis_entries.anchor: note was immediately despatched, and its contents as quickly complied with.
analysis_entries.note: The speed with which the note is dispatched and the visit arranged underscores the proximity and social expectations of the neighborhood, while also hinting at Mrs. Bennet's eagerness to keep Jane at Netherfield.

Mrs. Bennet's profuse gratitude often borders on servility when dealing with those of higher status, like Bingley, which serves to highlight her lack of social poise compared to her daughter Elizabeth.

Elizabeth's claim to understand Bingley 'perfectly' signals the start of a genuine friendship based on mutual openness and wit, contrasting with the layered deceits often found in Regency social interactions.

analysis_entries.anchor: wild manner that you are suffered to do at home.
analysis_entries.note: Mrs. Bennet’s rebuke of Elizabeth’s 'wild manner' is ironic, as the mother herself is far more socially erratic, illustrating the lack of self-awareness that plagues the older Bennet generation.

Darcy's silent withdrawal from Mrs. Bennet's argument is his primary defense against social inferiority; he chooses not to engage with those he deems beneath him, which Elizabeth interprets as intolerable pride.
The debate on poetry as the 'food of love' allows Austen to explore the intellectual compatibility between Elizabeth and Darcy, as they spar using metaphors that reveal their differing temperaments.

analysis_entries.anchor: insist on their giving one also.
analysis_entries.note: Lydia's insistence on the ball introduces her character’s primary drive: a reckless pursuit of pleasure and social attention, which will eventually lead to the novel's central crisis.

quote_entries.anchor: Whatever I do is done in a hurry
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Bingley’s Disposition">“Whatever I do is done in a hurry,” replied he; “and therefore if I should resolve to quit Netherfield, I should probably be off in five minutes.”</Callout>
<Callout variant="quote" title="The Amusing Study">“Yes; but intricate characters are the _most_ amusing. They have at least that advantage.”</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: few subjects for such a study.
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Darcy’s View of the Country">“The country,” said Darcy, “can in general supply but few subjects for such a study. In a country neighbourhood you move in a very confined and unvarying society.”</Callout>
<Callout variant="quote" title="The Food of Love">“I have been used to consider poetry as the _food_ of love,” said Darcy.</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: one good sonnet will starve it entirely away.
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="The Efficacy of Poetry">“But if it be only a slight, thin sort of inclination, I am convinced that one good sonnet will starve it entirely away.</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: shameful thing in the world if he did not keep it.
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Lydia’s Bold Request">“She was very equal, therefore, to address Mr. Bingley on the subject of the ball, and abruptly reminded him of his promise; adding, that it would be the most shameful thing in the world if he did not keep it.”</Callout>
<Callout variant="quote" title="Darcy’s Quiet Resistance">“He could not be prevailed on to join in their censure of _her_, in spite of all Miss Bingley’s witticisms on _fine eyes_.”</Callout>
